Acts 1.audience: Luke writes again to Theophilus, picking up from "the former treatise" (Acts 1:1). Acts follows the apostles from Jerusalem to Rome.

culture.title: A sabbath day's journey
culture.text: The distance a person could walk on the sabbath, about 2,000 cubits (roughly two-thirds of a mile).

culture.title: The upper room
culture.text: Upper rooms were built on the flat roofs of larger houses and could hold a sizable group.

culture.title: Casting lots
culture.text: Lots were used to make decisions left to God (Proverbs 16:33), including priestly duties (Luke 1:9).

Acts 2.audience: Readers who knew that pilgrims from a dozen distant regions normally could not understand each other without a shared trade language would have recognized the crowd's ability to hear the apostles in their own native tongues as a deliberate reversal of the confusion at Babel.

culture.title: Pentecost
culture.text: Pentecost (‘fiftieth’) is the feast of weeks, fifty days after Passover, celebrating the wheat harvest (Leviticus 23:15–21).

culture.title: The third hour
culture.text: About 9 a.m., the hour of morning prayer, too early for drunkenness.

culture.title: Breaking bread from house to house
culture.text: Believers met in the temple courts and shared meals in homes.

Acts 3.audience: Peter and John heal a lame man at the temple gate and Peter speaks in Solomon's porch.

culture.title: The hour of prayer
culture.text: The ninth hour (about 3 p.m.) was the time of the evening sacrifice and prayer.

culture.title: The gate called Beautiful
culture.text: Josephus describes a temple gate of Corinthian bronze, which may be this gate. Beggars sat where worshipers passed.

Acts 4.audience: Readers who knew that the same priestly family had handed Jesus over to Pilate only weeks earlier would have recognized Peter and John facing that very court as picking up a confrontation the authorities likely hoped had ended with the crucifixion.

culture.title: The captain of the temple
culture.text: The captain of the temple was a senior priest in charge of the temple police.

culture.title: Unlearned and ignorant men
culture.text: The word translated ‘unlearned’ described someone without formal scribal training.

culture.title: Barnabas
culture.text: Joses, a Levite from Cyprus, is given the name Barnabas, which Luke translates "The son of consolation."

Acts 5.audience: Ananias and Sapphira die after lying about their gift. The apostles are arrested again, and Gamaliel advises the council to leave them alone.

culture.title: Gamaliel
culture.text: Gamaliel was a leading Pharisee teacher, remembered in Jewish tradition as Rabban Gamaliel the Elder. Paul studied under him (Acts 22:3).

culture.title: Theudas and Judas of Galilee
culture.text: Josephus describes Judas the Galilean, who led a revolt over the census of AD 6, and a Theudas who led a movement later.

culture.title: Beaten
culture.text: The law limited a beating to forty stripes (Deuteronomy 25:3); in practice thirty-nine were given (2 Corinthians 11:24).

Acts 6.audience: Readers who knew that Greek-speaking and Aramaic-speaking Jews worshiped and organized charity somewhat separately even within the same city would have recognized the apostles' solution, appointing leaders with Greek names to fix a Greek-speaking community's complaint, as a deliberately even-handed response rather than a token gesture.

culture.title: Grecians and Hebrews
culture.text: Grecians were Jews from outside the land who spoke Greek; Hebrews spoke Aramaic and were from Judea or Galilee.

culture.title: The synagogue of the Libertines
culture.text: Libertines were freedmen, perhaps descendants of Jews enslaved by Rome. A Greek inscription found in Jerusalem records a synagogue built by Theodotus for visitors from abroad.

Acts 7.audience: Stephen reviews Israel's history from Abraham to Solomon before the council and is stoned. Saul watches the coats of the witnesses (Acts 7:58).

culture.title: The learning of the Egyptians
culture.text: This detail about Moses' education does not appear in Exodus but is also found in Philo and Josephus.

culture.title: Stoning outside the city
culture.text: Executions took place outside the camp or city, and the witnesses threw the first stones (Deuteronomy 17:7).

Acts 8.audience: Readers who knew that Jews and Samaritans normally avoided each other, and that a court official from a distant African kingdom would have had almost no access to a private Jewish teacher otherwise, would have recognized both encounters as crossing boundaries the gospel had not yet crossed in Jerusalem.

culture.title: Simon the sorcerer
culture.text: Magicians who claimed special powers were common in the Roman world. The word "simony" (buying church office) comes from this Simon.

culture.title: Candace
culture.text: Candace (Kandake) was a title for the queen mother of the kingdom of Meroë, in modern Sudan, not a personal name.

culture.title: Reading aloud
culture.text: Reading was usually done aloud, so Philip could hear the official reading Isaiah.

Acts 9.audience: Saul, sent with letters to arrest believers in Damascus, sees Jesus on the road. Peter heals Aeneas and raises Tabitha.

culture.title: Letters to Damascus
culture.text: The high priest's letters gave Saul authority with Damascus' synagogues, which had large Jewish communities.

culture.title: The street called Straight
culture.text: Damascus' main east–west street still follows the line of the Roman road.

culture.title: Let down in a basket
culture.text: Paul describes the same escape in 2 Corinthians 11:32–33.

Acts 10.audience: Peter sees a vision of unclean animals and goes to the house of Cornelius, a Roman centurion, in Caesarea.

culture.title: The Italian band
culture.text: A cohort of about 600 soldiers. Caesarea was the Roman capital of Judea.

culture.title: Simon a tanner
culture.text: Tanning used animal hides and was considered unclean work, often done by the sea outside town.

culture.title: Unlawful to keep company
culture.text: Many Jews avoided entering Gentile houses or eating with Gentiles to keep the food and purity laws.

Acts 11.audience: Peter defends his visit to Cornelius in Jerusalem. The church in Antioch grows, and the disciples are first called Christians there (Acts 11:26).

culture.title: Antioch
culture.text: Antioch in Syria was one of the largest cities in the Roman Empire, with a large Jewish population.

culture.title: Christians
culture.text: The name means ‘followers of Christ’; the -ianus ending is Latin, like ‘Herodians.’

culture.title: Famine under Claudius
culture.text: Roman writers record several food shortages under Claudius (AD 41–54), and Josephus a famine in Judea around AD 46–48.

Acts 12.audience: Readers who remembered Peter's earlier escape from a Jerusalem jail (Acts 5:19) would have recognized this second angelic rescue, and Herod's own sudden death shortly after accepting worship as a god, as framing the chapter's real contrast between a king's claimed power and its actual limits.

culture.title: Four quaternions
culture.text: Sixteen soldiers in four squads guarded Peter, one squad for each watch of the night.

culture.title: Mary's house
culture.text: Mary, mother of John Mark, owned a house large enough for a gathering, with a gate and a servant girl, Rhoda.

culture.title: Herod's death
culture.text: Josephus also records that Agrippa died suddenly at Caesarea in AD 44 after the crowd hailed him as a god.

Acts 13.audience: The church at Antioch sends Barnabas and Saul to Cyprus and southern Galatia. From here Saul is called Paul (Acts 13:9).

culture.title: Sergius Paulus
culture.text: Cyprus was a senatorial province, governed by a proconsul ("deputy"). Inscriptions mention men named Sergius Paullus.

culture.title: Reading the law and the prophets
culture.text: Synagogue services included readings from the law and the prophets, after which visitors could be asked to speak.

culture.title: Devout and honourable women
culture.text: Gentile women of high standing were often drawn to the synagogue.

Acts 14.audience: In Lystra, the crowd takes Barnabas and Paul for gods; then Paul is stoned. They return, appointing elders in each church.

culture.title: The speech of Lycaonia
culture.text: The crowd speaks their local language, so Paul and Barnabas don't understand at first.

culture.title: Jupiter and Mercurius
culture.text: Zeus and Hermes. Ovid tells a legend of the two gods visiting nearby Phrygia in disguise, and inscriptions near Lystra honor both together.

culture.title: Oxen and garlands
culture.text: Sacrificial animals were decorated with wreaths before being offered.

Acts 15.audience: Readers who knew that circumcision was the single clearest marker separating Jews from Gentiles in the ancient world would have recognized how much was actually being decided when the Jerusalem council chose not to require it of new Gentile believers.

culture.title: Things strangled and blood
culture.text: Leviticus 17–18 gives similar rules on blood, eating animals not properly drained, and sexual relations, applying also to foreigners living in Israel.

culture.title: Moses read every sabbath
culture.text: The law was read every sabbath in synagogues across the Roman world.

culture.title: Letters
culture.text: The letter follows the standard Greek form: senders, recipients, "greeting," and "Fare ye well" at the end.

Acts 16.audience: Paul takes Timothy, crosses to Macedonia, and founds the church in Philippi. Luke starts writing "we" here (Acts 16:10).

culture.title: Philippi, a colony
culture.text: Philippi was a Roman colony settled by veterans, governed under Roman law and proud of its Roman citizenship.

culture.title: A seller of purple
culture.text: Thyatira was known for its dyeing trade; inscriptions there mention guilds of dyers.

culture.title: Romans beaten uncondemned
culture.text: Roman citizens were protected from beating without trial; the magistrates had broken the law.

Acts 17.audience: Readers who knew that Thessalonica, Berea, and Athens each had a very different kind of audience, a Jewish synagogue, an unusually open synagogue, and a civic council of philosophers, would have recognized Paul adjusting his method each time while never changing his actual message.

culture.title: Politarchs
culture.text: The "rulers of the city" are politarchs in Greek, a title found in inscriptions from Thessalonica.

culture.title: Epicureans and Stoics
culture.text: Two main philosophical schools: Epicureans valued tranquility and believed the gods were distant; Stoics taught living by reason and divine order.

culture.title: To the unknown god
culture.text: Ancient writers mention altars in Athens to unknown gods. Paul quotes Greek poets, including Aratus (Acts 17:28).

Acts 18.audience: Readers who knew that Jewish tentmakers and artisans often formed close working partnerships that doubled as lodging arrangements would have recognized Paul's extended stay with Aquila and Priscilla as both an economic and a teaching relationship, not simply a long visit.

culture.title: Claudius expels the Jews
culture.text: The Roman historian Suetonius records that Claudius expelled Jews from Rome because of disturbances, around AD 49.

culture.title: Tentmakers
culture.text: Tentmakers worked in leather and cloth. Rabbis were expected to learn a trade.

culture.title: Gallio
culture.text: An inscription found at Delphi dates Gallio's term as proconsul of Achaia to about AD 51–52.

Acts 19.audience: Paul spends over two years in Ephesus. A silversmith stirs up a riot in the theater over the goddess Diana.

culture.title: Burning magic books
culture.text: Ephesus was known for magical texts, called ‘Ephesian letters.’ The books burned were worth fifty thousand pieces of silver.

culture.title: Diana of the Ephesians
culture.text: Diana (Artemis) had a temple at Ephesus that was one of the Seven Wonders of the World.

culture.title: The theatre
culture.text: Ephesus' excavated theater could seat about 24,000 people.

Acts 20.audience: Readers who knew how unusual it was for a traveling teacher to bypass a city entirely rather than risk the delay of a proper visit would have felt the urgency behind Paul calling the Ephesian elders to meet him at the port instead, rather than go to them himself.

culture.title: The first day of the week
culture.text: Believers in Troas gathered on the first day of the week to break bread.

culture.title: Many lights
culture.text: The meeting was in a third-floor room (Acts 20:9) lit by many oil lamps.

culture.title: Falling on his neck
culture.text: Embracing and kissing was a common farewell (Genesis 33:4).

Acts 21.audience: Readers who knew that the Antonia fortress stood right beside the temple specifically so Roman troops could respond within minutes to any disturbance in the courts below would have recognized how quickly, and how routinely, that rescue happened.

culture.title: Paying for vows
culture.text: A Nazarite vow ended with shaving the head and offering sacrifices (Numbers 6:13–18).

culture.title: Gentiles in the temple
culture.text: Stone inscriptions warned Gentiles not to pass the barrier into the inner courts on pain of death; two have been found.

culture.title: The castle
culture.text: The Antonia fortress at the northwest corner of the temple housed a Roman garrison, with stairs down into the temple courts.

Acts 22.audience: Readers who knew that Roman law normally allowed a citizen facing examination to invoke that status before being struck, not after, would have recognized how perilously close the soldiers had already come to breaking the law before Paul spoke up.

culture.title: Brought up at Gamaliel's feet
culture.text: Students sat at their teacher's feet.

culture.title: Freeborn
culture.text: Citizenship could be bought, granted, or inherited. Paul was born a citizen.

culture.title: Scourging
culture.text: Romans flogged suspects to get confessions. Beating a citizen without trial was illegal.

Acts 23.audience: Paul appears before the Sanhedrin. A plot against him leads the commander to send him to Felix at Caesarea.

culture.title: Ananias the high priest
culture.text: Josephus describes Ananias, high priest about AD 47–59, as greedy and violent.

culture.title: Pharisees and Sadducees
culture.text: Luke explains that the Sadducees deny resurrection, angels, and spirits, but the Pharisees believe in all three.

culture.title: Claudius Lysias' letter
culture.text: The letter follows the Greek form: sender, "unto the most excellent governor Felix," greeting.

Acts 24.audience: The orator Tertullus accuses Paul before Felix, who keeps him in custody for two years hoping for a bribe (Acts 24:26–27).

culture.title: Flattering the governor
culture.text: Speeches often began with praise of the judge. Roman historian Tacitus says Felix ruled with cruelty and lust.

culture.title: Drusilla
culture.text: Drusilla was a daughter of Herod Agrippa I. She left her first husband to marry Felix.

Acts 25.audience: Festus replaces Felix. Paul appeals to Caesar, and Festus consults King Agrippa.

culture.title: Appeal to Caesar
culture.text: Roman citizens could appeal a case to the emperor, at this time Nero.

culture.title: Agrippa and Bernice
culture.text: Herod Agrippa II, son of Agrippa I, ruled territories to the north and east. Bernice was his sister.

Acts 26.audience: Paul tells Agrippa about his life and conversion. Agrippa and Festus agree that he could have been released if he had not appealed to Caesar (Acts 26:32).

culture.title: Stretching forth the hand
culture.text: Orators raised their hand as a gesture when starting a speech.

culture.title: Kicking against the pricks
culture.text: Oxen kicking against a goad hurt only themselves; the saying also appears in Greek writers.

culture.title: Done in a corner
culture.text: A Greek phrase for something done in secret.

Acts 27.audience: Paul sails for Rome under a centurion named Julius and is shipwrecked on Malta. Luke describes the journey in detail as an eyewitness ("we").

culture.title: Ships of Alexandria
culture.text: Large grain ships carried wheat from Egypt to Rome and also took passengers.

culture.title: The fast
culture.text: The fast of the Day of Atonement came in late September or October. Sailing became dangerous from mid-September and stopped for the winter.

culture.title: Undergirding the ship
culture.text: Sailors passed cables under the hull to hold it together in a storm.

Acts 28.audience: Readers who knew that a prisoner awaiting trial in Rome normally had far less freedom than renting his own lodging and receiving all who came to him would have recognized how unusually open Paul's two years of custody actually were.

culture.title: Castor and Pollux
culture.text: The ship's figurehead was the twin gods, considered protectors of sailors.

culture.title: Appii forum and The three taverns
culture.text: Stops on the Appian Way, about 43 and 33 miles south of Rome.

culture.title: House arrest
culture.text: Paul is allowed to live alone with a soldier guarding him, probably chained to him (Acts 28:20).
